title: Louisiana Attorney General Opinion 13-0054 (2013-08-13)
text:
August 13, 2013
OPINION 13-0054
71-1-B MUNICIPALITIES- Home Rule Charter
La.Const. art. VI, § 5
Livingston Parish Ordinance No. 13-16, relating to the appointment
and approval power for directors and department heads, conflicts
Mr. Layton Ricks with the Livingston Parish Home Rule Charter and should be
considered invalid and without legal effect.
Livingston Parish President
P.O. Box 427
Livingston, Louisiana 70754
Dear Mr. Ricks:
Our office received your request for an opinion on whether Livingston Parish Ordinance
No. 13-16 violates the Livingston Parish Home Rule Charter (“Charter”). On May 9,
2013, a public hearing was held, and the Livingston Parish Council (“Council”) adopted
Livingston Parish Ordinance No. 13-16 (“Ordinance”) which adds Sections 2-17, 2-17.1,
2-17.2, 2-17.3, and 2-17.4 to the Livingston Parish Code of Ordinances (a copy of the
Ordinance has been attached to this opinion). The Ordinance defines “director” and
“department head” as interchangeable terms which refer to the most senior
management individual within a department. The stated intent of the Ordinance is to
describe the appointment process of directors in detail and to ensure that the Council
has final approval of parish directors and department heads appointed by the Parish
President (“President”). The Ordinance also sets forth a selection and approval process
for parish directors and department heads, and states that it is retroactive to January 1,
2013. You have asked whether this Ordinance conflicts with the Charter, and if so,
what effect a conflicting ordinance would have.
Livingston Parish operates pursuant to a home rule charter adopted under the authority
of Article VI, § 5 of the Louisiana Constitution. The plan of government is “president-
council” whereby the President serves as the chief executive officer and head of the
executive branch and the Council constitutes the legislative branch.1
Section 3-09 of the Charter sets forth the powers and duties of the President and states
that the President, as chief executive officer, shall have the power to “appoint and
suspend or remove for just cause all employees and appointive administrative officers
provided for by or under this charter, except as otherwise provided….”
1 Charter, Section 1-02.

Section 4-01 of the Charter states in pertinent part:
A. Except as otherwise provided by this charter, all departments, offices,
and agencies shall be under the direction and supervision of the president.
The directors of all departments created by or under this charter
shall be appointed by the president subject to council approval, and
shall serve at the pleasure of the president.
[Emphasis added].
Under Section 4-01 of the Charter, the directors of departments which are created by or
under the Charter are to be appointed by the President, subject to Council approval.
This appointment process encompasses all parish government departments that were
in existence on the effective date of the Charter, as well as parish departments created
thereafter, pursuant to Section 4-07 of the Charter.2
Ordinance No. 13-16 states that if the Parish President does not find qualified personnel
to fill a director position within 60 days, then he must explain the delay to the Council
and ask for additional time to fill the vacancy. If the President has not filled the vacancy
within 120 days, then the vacant director position is automatically abolished and the
duties assigned to another individual within the Parish Administration. The Ordinance
attempts to transfer the authority to appoint department directors from the President to
the Council. Under the Ordinance, the Council simply has to vote against approving the
appointee(s) proposed by the President for a period of 120 days, after which the Council
is allowed to abolish the position and assign the duties to someone else in the
administration without the President’s appointment or input. While the Council has the
authority to approve or reject the President’s appointment, the fact that the position is
vacant for a certain number of days does not grant the Council the ability to usurp the
executive's authority to appoint a department director. This seizure of the executive’s
power by the Council conflicts with Sections 3-09 and 4-01 of the Charter.
Further, the Ordinance attempts to grant the Council the power to abolish certain
government positions without the consent of the President. Section 4-06 of the Charter
requires that “all government departments, offices, agencies, and functions in existence
on the effective date of this charter shall continue in existence as organized on that date
until reorganized in accordance with the section on ‘Administrative Reorganization.’”
Section 4-07 of the Charter sets forth the procedure for administrative reorganization
and states that “abolishment of parish departments, offices, agencies, and/or the
reallocation of the functions, powers, duties and responsibilities of such departments,
offices or agencies” may take place when proposed by the President. Once the
2 See Section 4-06 of the Charter which provides: “Except as otherwise provided by this charter, all
government departments, offices, agencies, and functions in existence on the effective date of this
charter shall continue in existence as organized on that date until reorganized in accordance with the
section on “Administrative Reorganization.’” Section 4-07 also permits the creation of new parish
departments under the Charter.

Mr. Layton Ricks

proposal is made by the President, the Council votes on whether to accept the proposal
and may make changes to the proposed reorganization plan with the consent of the
President.3 To the extent the Ordinance attempts to grant the Council the additional
power to abolish a position that was in effect on the effective date of the Charter, it is in
conflict with Sections 4-06 and 4-07 of the Charter, which clearly set forth the exclusive
procedure for reorganization. Any change in the organizational makeup of the parish
plan of government must be accomplished through the process set forth in Section 7-03
of the Charter and not by passage of an ordinance.
Our office has consistently taken the position that when an ordinance violates or
conflicts with the home rule charter, the ordinance must be stricken and declared
invalid.4 It is the opinion of our office that Ordinance No. 13-16 is in conflict with
Sections 3-09, 4-10, 4-06, and 4-07 of the Charter and should be considered invalid and
without legal effect.
We hope that this opinion has adequately addressed the legal issues you have raised.
If our office can be of any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact us.
With best regards,
JAMES D. “BUDDY” CALDWELL
ATTORNEY GENERAL
